text: Write the entire history of nigeria in the style of NAME_1
answer:
# THE HISTORY OF NIGERIA
*as told in the style of* ***Terry Pratchett***

---

## Being a Mostly Accurate Account of a Very Large Country That Had the Misfortune of Being Interesting to Almost Everyone

---

There is a place in the world — and the world, being the sort of place it is, has rather a lot of places in it — where the land does something remarkable. It takes a perfectly good river, the Niger, and another perfectly good river, the Benue, and crashes them together in a sort of geographical argument that has never quite been resolved, creating a delta so enormous and so wet that it has opinions about things.

This place is Nigeria.

It is, by most measurable standards, enormous. It contains approximately two hundred million people, which is more people than any other country in Africa, a fact that Nigeria mentions at parties and other countries pretend not to have heard. It contains over five hundred languages, which means that the arguments about what anything means can last considerably longer than the things being argued about.

It has oil.

This last fact is important. We will return to it. We always return to it. Like a bad smell or an interesting relative, it keeps showing up.

---

## PART ONE: THE BEGINNING (Before Anyone Wrote Anything Down, Which Made It Harder For Everyone Later)

In the beginning — which is to say, several hundred thousand years before anyone invented the concept of Nigeria — the land was occupied by people who had the excellent good sense to live where there was water, food, and a reasonable absence of things trying to eat them.

The Nok people, who flourished around 1500 BCE to 200 CE, were particularly impressive. They worked iron at a time when most of the world was still getting to grips with bronze, which is the sort of thing that should earn you considerable historical respect but mostly earns you a paragraph in textbooks and a display case in a museum in Jos.

They made terracotta sculptures. The sculptures had hollow eyes and detailed hairstyles, which suggests that the Nok people had, like all sensible civilizations, figured out that (a) art matters and (b) hair matters, possibly even more than art.

The terracotta figures stare out from their museum cases with an expression that can only be described as *we were here first and we had style*.

They were not wrong.

---

Meanwhile, in the north, empires were happening.

Empires, it should be noted, are what occur when someone with organizational ability meets someone with ambition and they both decide that other people's resources belong to them, philosophically speaking.

The **Kanem-Bornu Empire** began around the ninth century CE and lasted, with the sort of stubborn persistence that empires occasionally display, until the nineteenth century. This is over a thousand years, which puts it in the category of Things That Lasted Longer Than They Had Any Right To, alongside the Roman Senate, certain bureaucracies, and particularly determined aunts.

Kanem-Bornu sat astride the trans-Saharan trade routes, which meant it was excellently positioned to tax things. Taxing things is the foundation of civilization. Anyone who tells you civilization was founded on art or philosophy has not studied enough history.

The **Hausa Kingdoms** — Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir, and others — were city-states of considerable sophistication. Kano in particular was a center of learning, trade, and the production of leather goods so fine that they were exported all the way to North Africa and known in Europe, where they were called "Morocco leather," which is the sort of geographical attribution error that trade has always been very good at making.

The Hausa cities had walls. Very large walls. The walls of Kano were fourteen miles in circumference and up to fifty feet high in places, which means the people who built them had either a great many enemies or a great deal of ambition, and possibly both.

---

## PART TWO: KINGDOMS IN THE SOUTH (Where the Forest Had Opinions)

In the southwest, the **Yoruba** people built something remarkable: a network of city-states organized around the concept of the **Oyo Empire**, which at its height in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries controlled territory stretching from what is now Nigeria into what is now Benin, in a display of imperial reach that the geography had not entirely consented to.

The Yoruba had a cosmology of extraordinary complexity. They had **401 orishas** — divine beings who managed various aspects of the universe — which is considerably more divine management than most religions attempt, and suggests either a very complicated universe or a very detailed theology, or possibly both.

**Ogun** managed iron and war. **Shango** managed thunder and lightning and was known for having a somewhat volatile personality, which is more or less what you'd expect from a god of thunder. **Oshun** managed rivers and love and prosperity. **Eshu** managed crossroads and communication and was the divine trickster, which meant that he was often blamed for things going wrong, which is the traditional fate of anyone associated with communication.

The **Ife** civilization, ancestral home of Yoruba culture, produced bronze and brass sculptures of such technical and artistic brilliance in the twelfth to fifteenth centuries that when European archaeologists first encountered them in the late nineteenth century, several of them refused to believe Africans had made them and attributed them to ancient Egyptians, or Phoenicians, or occasionally Atlantis.

This tells you rather more about the archaeologists than it does about the sculptures.

The sculptures were, and remain, extraordinary.

---

In the south, in the dense forests and the swampy delta, the **Kingdom of Benin** — not to be confused with the modern country next door, which chose its name in a moment of historical enthusiasm — was doing something important with bronze.

The Benin Bronzes are, technically, brasses, which is the kind of correction that annoys everyone and pleases nobody, but accuracy has its obligations. These plaques and sculptures decorated the royal palace of the **Oba** of Benin with images of court life, warriors, royalty, and the occasional leopard, who appears to have been considered significant.

The Oba was a divine king. His foot was not supposed to touch the ground. His face was not supposed to be seen eating. These rules, like most rules surrounding divine kingship, were partly about religious observance and partly about maintaining an air of mystery, which is easier to do if you are not observed chewing.

The Kingdom of Benin was, by the standards of anywhere, impressive.

It will come up again, unfortunately.

---

In the southeast, the **Igbo** people had chosen a different approach entirely. Instead of building large centralized kingdoms, they had built something considerably more interesting: a culture of **participatory governance**, in which villages were organized around councils, elders, and the voices of women through the **Omu** institution, without requiring a king at all.

This is the sort of organizational choice that political philosophers would later spend a great deal of time admiring from a safe historical distance.

The Igbo also had the **Arochukwu** oracle, the **Ibini Ukpabi**, known to outsiders as the "Long Juju," which served as a religious, legal, and diplomatic institution of considerable authority across a wide area. People came from hundreds of miles to have their disputes settled by an oracle, which is considerably more efficient than a court system and probably produced similar results.

---

## PART THREE: TRANS-SAHARAN TRADE, AND WHY SALT IS MORE IMPORTANT THAN YOU THINK

For centuries, caravans crossed the Sahara Desert, which is the sort of thing that sounds romantic until you consider the temperatures involved.

They carried gold going north. They carried salt going south.

Salt, it must be understood, was not merely a condiment. Salt was survival. Salt was preservation. Salt was, in the economies of sub-Saharan Africa, essentially money. The Saharan trade routes exchanged Saharan salt for West African gold in proportions that made both sides feel they were getting a reasonable deal, which is the ideal outcome of any trade and is considerably rarer than it sounds.

The Islamic world, having conveniently expanded across North Africa in the seventh and eighth centuries, provided the markets, the merchants, the credit systems, and eventually the religion that traveled along these routes.

Islam arrived in the Hausa states and Kanem-Bornu not with armies but with merchants and scholars, which is a considerably more persuasive combination than armies in the long run. By the fifteenth century, the rulers of the major northern states were Muslim, Islamic learning was flourishing in cities like Katsina and Kano, and a scholarly tradition was established that would later produce the library collections of Timbuktu's slightly-more-famous neighbor and produce scholars of considerable sophistication.

The south, protected from the trade routes by the forest and the tsetse fly — which is a small insect that has had an enormous effect on African history by making horses die — remained largely outside the Islamic sphere.

Geography, as usual, had opinions.

---

## PART FOUR: THE ATLANTIC TRADE (A Chapter That Requires Some Preparation)

In 1472, Portuguese sailors arrived on the coast of what would become Nigeria.

This is the kind of sentence that appears simple and contains multitudes.

The Portuguese were, in the fifteenth century, engaged in an ambitious project of sailing around the coast of Africa in order to reach the trade goods of Asia without going through the Middle East, which was inconveniently controlled by people who wanted to charge tariffs. This is, when you think about it, a very European thing to do: go the long way around to avoid paying someone fairly.

Initial contact was trade. The Portuguese traded in pepper, cloth, and later slaves. The Kingdom of Benin traded carefully and selectively, and for a while traded in male slaves while refusing to trade in women, a distinction that seems almost thoughtful in retrospect but was not, ultimately, a meaningful limit on the catastrophe that was unfolding.

Because here is what happened next:

The Spanish and Portuguese had colonized the Caribbean and were developing sugar plantations on a vast scale. Sugar required labor. They had decided, through a combination of economics and moral failure of absolutely breathtaking proportions, that this labor would be enslaved African people.

Between approximately 1500 and 1850, somewhere between 3.5 million and 4 million people were taken from the territory that is now Nigeria and transported across the Atlantic Ocean in conditions of deliberate brutality to work on plantations in Brazil, the Caribbean, and North America.

This is not a number. These are people. They had names. They had families. They had languages and religions and cosmologies with 401 gods and iron-working traditions and oral histories and plans for the future.

The Yoruba diaspora shaped the religious life of Brazil, Cuba, and Trinidad. The Igbo diaspora shaped the culture of Virginia and the Caribbean. The Hausa diaspora produced soldiers and rebels and scholars in conditions designed to prevent all three.

The slave trade did not merely remove people. It reorganized the political economy of the entire region around the business of capturing and selling people, which meant that states that participated in the trade grew powerful and states that didn't grew vulnerable, which meant that eventually almost everyone participated, which is how a moral catastrophe becomes a structural one.

The Oyo Empire participated extensively. The Aro Network of the Igbo participated. Various coastal kingdoms participated. They were not passive victims; they were also active agents in a system that was, ultimately, grinding everyone down, and this is one of the complicated true things about history that requires you to hold several contradictory thoughts at once without breaking.

---

## PART FIVE: THE JIHAD (IN WHICH THINGS REORGANIZE THEMSELVES)

In 1804, a Fulani Islamic scholar named **Usman dan Fodio** declared a jihad.

Usman dan Fodio was a serious man. He had spent years teaching, writing, and being increasingly annoyed by the Hausa rulers who claimed to be Muslim while doing things he considered incompatible with proper Islamic governance, including, among other things, taxing the poor excessively and behaving in ways that struck him as more interested in power than in piety.

This is a complaint that has been made about rulers approximately since the invention of rulers, but Usman dan Fodio had followers, charisma, and the organizational ability to do something about it.

The jihad swept through the Hausa kingdoms with considerable speed. Within a few years, the old Hausa ruling dynasties were overthrown and replaced by Fulani emirs operating within a new structure: the **Sokoto Caliphate**.

The Sokoto Caliphate became the largest state in Africa south of the Sahara in the nineteenth century. It was an Islamic state, seriously so, with a genuine commitment to scholarship, justice, and the proper organization of social life according to Islamic law — though, as with all states committed to justice, the distance between the aspiration and the practice varied.

It was also, unfortunately, a state that practiced slavery extensively, which is one of the historical facts that requires holding alongside everything else.

The Sokoto Caliphate would remain the dominant power in northern Nigeria until 1903, when it had a significant disagreement with the British Empire. The British Empire, as we shall see, had developed by this point.

---

## PART SIX: THE BRITISH ARRIVE (And Decide Everything Is Theirs)

The British had been present on the Nigerian coast in various capacities since the seventeenth century. They had traded in slaves, which they now publicly regretted, and had declared the slave trade illegal in 1807, which was morally significant and practically complicated, given that abolishing the trade while the underlying economic demand remained required the Royal Navy to patrol an entire ocean, which it did, with characteristic thoroughness.

The British established Lagos as a colony in 1861, nominally to suppress the slave trade, actually because Lagos was an excellent port and ports are worth having. This is the standard British explanation for most of their colonial acquisitions: they were protecting trade, or suppressing evil practices, or responding to requests for assistance that they had sometimes arranged to receive.

The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 is one of those historical events that you need to sit down for. European powers — Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Portugal, and others — met in Berlin to divide Africa among themselves. Africa was not invited to this meeting. Africa's opinion on the matter was not solicited. The European powers drew lines on maps, agreed on spheres of influence, and went home satisfied with a job well done.

The job they had done was decide that the entire continent belonged to them, which was, by the standards of either law or logic, simply not true, but when you have sufficient guns the question of what is true becomes temporarily subordinate to the question of what you can enforce.

Britain claimed the area that would become Nigeria.

---

**Frederick Lugard** is a name that anyone who wants to understand modern Nigeria needs to know, and having learned it, will probably wish they could unknow it.

Lugard was a British soldier and colonial administrator who conquered the Sokoto Caliphate in 1903 — the Caliph was killed, the Emirs who submitted were allowed to keep their positions under British oversight, and the ones who didn't were replaced — and who in 1914 amalgamated the Northern Nigeria Protectorate and the Southern Nigeria Protectorate into the **Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria**.

The amalgamation was primarily an administrative convenience. It reduced the costs of running two separate bureaucracies. The people being administered were not extensively consulted about whether they wished to be a single administrative unit.

They did not wish to be a single administrative unit, in the main, but their wishes were, at this stage, considered secondary to the logistics of colonial administration.

Lugard is famous for developing the policy of **Indirect Rule**, which was the observation that the British did not have enough people to run Nigeria directly, and therefore it was more efficient to use existing local rulers as intermediaries, allowing them to collect taxes, maintain order, and generally do the work of governing while the British sat at the top and cashed in.

This was praised as enlightened by the British and experienced as exploitation by most Nigerians. Both descriptions are accurate.

Indirect Rule worked reasonably well where there were existing hierarchical structures — the Hausa-Fulani emirates, for instance, were well suited to it. It worked considerably less well in Igbo areas, where the decentralized, non-hierarchical political tradition meant there were no "natural rulers" to work through, and the British therefore invented them, appointing Warrant Chiefs who had no traditional authority and were resented accordingly.

The resentment of the invented Warrant Chiefs would eventually lead to the **Women's War of 1929**, in which Igbo and Ibibio women, alarmed by a rumor that the British intended to tax women, organized protests across a vast area that the colonial authorities responded to by shooting into crowds, killing fifty women.

The women called it **Ogu Umunwanyi**. The British called it the Aba Riots, which reveals quite a lot about different perspectives on what constitutes a riot versus a war.

---

The colonial economy was organized, as colonial economies are, for the benefit of the colonizer.

Groundnuts in the north. Palm oil in the south. Cocoa in the southwest. Tin from the Jos Plateau. These were extracted, processed minimally, and shipped to Britain, where they were manufactured into things that were then sometimes sold back to Nigerians at a profit.

Railroads were built — not to connect Nigerian communities to each other but to connect the interior to the ports, because the point was extraction and the railroad was its instrument.

Taxes were levied in cash, which forced people into the cash economy, which meant they had to grow cash crops or seek wage labor, which meant they became economically dependent on the colonial system in ways that were no accident.

The British also ran the schools, which taught reading and writing and arithmetic and an understanding of history in which the British arrived and everything improved. The graduates of these schools would later use the reading and writing to write pamphlets, newspapers, and independence manifestos, which the British had not entirely anticipated.

---

## PART SEVEN: NATIONALISM (In Which People Read Books and Get Ideas)

The British educated Nigerians. This was, from the British point of view, intended to produce administrators, clerks, and people who would help run the colony. From the Nigerian point of view, it produced people who had read the works of John Stuart Mill on liberty and were prepared to point out that they applied universally.

**Herbert Macaulay** is often called the father of Nigerian nationalism. He was the grandson of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther, the first African Anglican bishop, which tells you something about the complexity of the colonial relationship. He founded a newspaper, organized political parties, and spent decades being annoying to the colonial authorities in a productive and principled way.

**Nnamdi Azikiwe** — "Zik" to everyone — studied in the United States, was influenced by Marcus Garvey and pan-African thought, returned to Nigeria, and proceeded to be the most effective newspaper editor and nationalist organizer of his generation. His newspapers were funny, sharp, and willing to say things that made colonial officials deeply uncomfortable, which is the highest praise a newspaper can receive.

**Obafemi Awolowo** — a Yoruba lawyer of extraordinary energy — organized the Action Group and became the leading proponent of federalism and regional autonomy. He had opinions about everything and was usually right about most of them, which is a quality that tends to make a person enemies.

**Ahmadu Bello**, the Sardauna of Sokoto and descendant of Usman dan Fodio, led the Northern People's Congress and represented the north's interests with considerable skill and a deep suspicion of the south's intentions, which were, to be fair, sometimes suspicious.

These three men — Azikiwe, Awolowo, Bello — represented the three major regions of Nigeria, which the British had organized along lines that more or less corresponded to the major ethnic and religious groupings: the Muslim, Hausa-Fulani north; the Yoruba southwest; the Igbo southeast.

This organization would prove to be one of the more consequential things the British did, and it had a great many competitors for that title.

---

## PART EIGHT: INDEPENDENCE (1960, WITH MIXED FEELINGS)

On October 1, 1960, Nigeria became independent.

This was celebrated with considerable enthusiasm, dancing, and optimism. The optimism was, in retrospect, partly justified and partly the kind of feeling you get when something long-awaited finally arrives and you haven't yet worked out what to do with it.

**Nnamdi Azikiwe** became Governor-General, later President. **Abubakar Tafawa Balewa**, a northern politician of honesty and moderation that was both his strength and, eventually, his vulnerability, became Prime Minister.

The structure of the new Nigeria was federal: three regions — North, East, West — with a central government. The regions were large and powerful. The north, in particular, was larger than France and had a majority of the population, which meant that in any democratic system the north would have structural advantages, which the south noticed and resented, and the north noticed being noticed and resented that.

The census of 1963 was, to put it plainly, fraudulent. Every region inflated its numbers to gain political advantage, and the official results were contested by everyone, including the people who had inflated their numbers, which is the kind of situation that does not inspire confidence in institutions.

The elections of 1964 and 1965 were also fraudulent, in a more alarming way. In the Western Region, an election was conducted with such creative mathematics and enthusiastic thuggery that the result satisfied nobody and was accepted by nobody, and violence spread across the region in a period known as **Operation Wetie** — Yoruba for "set on fire and wear the charcoal" — which tells you something about how bad it was.

---

## PART NINE: COUPS (There Were Several)

On January 15, 1966, a group of army officers launched a coup.

They killed Prime Minister Balewa. They killed the Premier of the Northern Region. They killed the Premier of the Western Region. They failed to kill President Azikiwe, who happened to be abroad for medical treatment.

The coup was led by Major Kaduna Nzeogwu and was, by the political geography of its victims, Igbo-dominated — most of the killed leaders were northern or western, most of the surviving leaders were Igbo — regardless of the genuine ideological motivations of some of its organizers.

The north noticed this.

**General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi**, an Igbo officer and the most senior surviving military commander, took power and established a military government. He issued Decree No. 34, which abolished the federal structure and unified the civil service, which the north interpreted as an Igbo power grab, which it was, in effect, regardless of intent.

Six months later, in July 1966, there was a counter-coup. Northern officers killed Ironsi. Soldiers in the north massacred Igbo civilians living in northern cities. The number killed was in the thousands. Igbo people fled the north.

**Yakubu Gowon**, a young northern officer of Christian middle-belt origins, which made him a somewhat acceptable compromise to everyone, took power.

He was thirty-one years old.

---

## PART TEN: THE CIVIL WAR (1967-1970)

The Governor of the Eastern Region was **Odumegwu Ojukwu**, an Igbo officer of considerable intelligence, charisma, and a magnificent beard. He argued that the federal government could not protect Igbo people, that the massacres had demonstrated this, and that the Igbo and other Eastern peoples had the right to their own state.

On May 30, 1967, Ojukwu declared the independent Republic of **Biafra**.

The name came from the Bight of Biafra, a stretch of the Atlantic coast. The new republic had a flag, an anthem, a currency, and an army. It also had oil, which was located in the Eastern Region and which made its secession an economic catastrophe for the rest of Nigeria and therefore made the federal government very serious indeed about preventing it.

The federal government had the advantages of size, international support — Britain and the Soviet Union both supported Nigeria; France and a few others supported Biafra; the United States declared neutrality and provided oil companies — and the ability to blockade the east.

The blockade of Biafra is where the war became something beyond a war. The federal government blockaded food. Children began to starve. **Kwashiorkor** — protein deficiency — produced the images of starving Biafran children with distended bellies and reddish hair that circulated around the world and provoked the modern tradition of international famine relief.

Between one and three million people died in the war, mostly Biafran civilians, mostly from starvation.

**The war ended on January 15, 1970.**

Gowon announced a policy of "No Victor, No Vanquished" and promised reconciliation. The Biafran soldiers were reintegrated. The death toll was not. The oil was reorganized under federal control, which was the important thing from the government's perspective, which tells you something about perspectives.

---

## PART ELEVEN: OIL (The Thing We've Been Building To)

In 1956, oil was discovered in the Niger Delta.

Oil had been suspected earlier. It was confirmed in 1956 at Oloibiri, in the region of the Ijaw people, near Port Harcourt, in a delta of mangrove swamps and waterways that is one of the most ecologically complex environments on earth.

By the 1970s, the oil price shock had made Nigerian oil extraordinarily valuable. The country was, briefly, spectacularly rich.

**Yakubu Gowon**, the young general, declared that Nigeria's problem was not money but how to spend it, which is the kind of statement that looks very different in retrospect.

The oil money produced infrastructure: refineries, steel mills, expressways, universities. It also produced corruption on an industrial scale, because when very large amounts of money move through government systems, some of it moves into pockets, and the larger the amounts, the larger the pockets required.

Gowon was overthrown in 1975 by **Murtala Mohammed**, who was energetic, decisive, and serious about cleaning up the government. He fired enormous numbers of corrupt civil servants and made a genuine impression on the country in his eight months in power before being assassinated in a coup attempt in February 1976.

**Olusegun Obasanjo** succeeded him and, remarkably, kept his promise to return to civilian rule. In 1979, elections were held. **Shehu Shagari** of the National Party of Nigeria became President.

The Second Republic lasted four years.

---

## PART TWELVE: MORE COUPS (The Army Had Opinions)

**Muhammadu Buhari** overthrew Shagari in December 1983, citing corruption, which was accurate, and economic mismanagement, which was also accurate, and which the coup planners were going to address by, among other things, imprisoning journalists for stories that embarrassed the government, which suggested their understanding of "mismanagement" was selective.

Buhari was overthrown by **Ibrahim Babangida** in 1985. Babangida, known as **IBB**, was a political operator of extraordinary cunning who ran Nigeria for eight years, promised transition to democracy approximately seventeen times, and delivered it approximately zero times before eventually, and under considerable pressure, stepping aside in 1993.

But before he stepped aside, there was the election of June 12, 1993.

**Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola** — **MKO Abiola** — a Yoruba businessman of considerable wealth, enormous generosity, and genuine popular support, won the election. The results, before they were fully counted, were annulled by Babangida.

The reasons given were procedural. The actual reason was that the military and its allies did not want Abiola to be president.

The annulment of June 12 is one of the defining wounds of Nigerian political history. It produced protests, strikes, and a pro-democracy movement of sustained intensity. Babangida installed an Interim National Government under **Ernest Shonekan**, which lasted approximately three months before **Sani Abacha**, the Defense Minister, removed it.

---

## PART THIRTEEN: ABACHA (A Dark Chapter)

**Sani Abacha** ruled Nigeria from 1993 to 1998.

He is one of those figures in history who is very easy to describe and very difficult to explain, because the description is so straightforwardly awful that it reads like a caricature, and yet he existed.

Abacha imprisoned Abiola, who had declared himself the rightful president. He imprisoned **Olusegun Obasanjo** on a charge of coup plotting. He imprisoned journalists, activists, politicians. He executed **Ken Saro-Wiwa**, the Ogoni writer and environmental activist, along with eight other Ogoni activists, in November 1995, following a trial described by international legal observers in terms that would require very impolite language to accurately reproduce.

Ken Saro-Wiwa had been protesting the environmental devastation of Ogoniland by oil extraction — specifically by Shell. The oil spills, the gas flaring, the destruction of farmland and fishing waters that had sustained the Ogoni people for generations. He had been doing this nonviolently and articulately and with considerable international attention.

He was hanged for it.

The international community expressed its horror. The Commonwealth suspended Nigeria. The Nigerian government noted this with apparent equanimity and continued.

Meanwhile, Abacha was stealing money. Not in small quantities. Subsequent investigations found that he had looted somewhere between three and five billion dollars from Nigerian state coffers, hidden in accounts across Europe.

In June 1998, Abacha died of a heart attack.

There are various versions of the circumstances of his death, none of which need to be detailed here, but which involve a social occasion in Abuja and leave the thoughtful observer to reflect on the traditional observation that history, while not exactly having a sense of humor, occasionally produces timing that is difficult not to notice.

---

## PART FOURTEEN: DEMOCRACY (The Third Attempt)

Abacha's death led, with remarkable speed given the previous thirty-five years, to a genuine transition to democracy.

**Olusegun Obasanjo** — released from prison the year before — won the presidential election of 1999. He was a former military dictator who had voluntarily handed over power in 1979, which made him, by Nigerian standards, almost uniquely qualified in virtue.

He served two terms. He attempted a third term via constitutional amendment, was prevented, and left office in 2007. The **transfer of power** was to **Umaru Yar'Adua**, a Katsina politician of quiet seriousness and genuine integrity, who was also seriously ill at the time of his election, which his party was aware of but did not mention, which was the kind of democratic irregularity that demonstrated democracy was being practiced with enthusiasm if not always rigor.

Yar'Adua died in office in 2010. **Goodluck Jonathan** — his Vice President, an Ijaw man from the Niger Delta, whose name is either the most optimistic or the most ironic in Nigerian political history depending on your perspective — became President.

Jonathan was elected in his own right in 2011 in an election considered the cleanest in Nigerian history, which gives some idea of the previous elections, but was nonetheless a genuine achievement.

In the Niger Delta, **Boko Haram** had been growing.

---

## PART FIFTEEN: BOKO HARAM (A Chapter That Requires Clarity)

**Boko Haram** — the name means, roughly, "Western education is forbidden," in Hausa — began as a religious movement in Maiduguri, in northeastern Nigeria, founded by **Mohammed Yusuf** in the early 2000s.

It was, initially, a movement of poor, young, and marginalized men in a region that had been failed by the Nigerian state in every measurable way. Education levels were low. Infrastructure was absent. Poverty was general. The grievances were real, which does not justify the response, but context is not excuse.

Mohammed Yusuf was killed by Nigerian police in 2009 in circumstances that suggest his captors were not interested in a trial. This turned a movement into an insurgency.

Under **Abubakar Shekau**, Boko Haram became one of the most violent extremist organizations in the world, by number of people killed. They attacked churches, mosques, schools, markets, villages. They killed soldiers and civilians without meaningful distinction. In April 2014, they kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, which produced **#BringBackOurGirls** and international attention and, for the girls, years of captivity.

The insurgency killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions. Lake Chad, once one of the great freshwater bodies of West Africa, had shrunk by ninety percent due to climate change and irrigation diversion, destroying the livelihoods of millions of people across the region, which had created exactly the conditions of desperation in which violent extremism flourishes.

The Nigerian military responded with operations that killed a great many people, not all of them insurgents, and displaced a great many more.

The situation remains unresolved.

---

## PART SIXTEEN: MUHAMMADU BUHARI (The Second Time)

In 2015, something happened that Nigerian democracy had never managed before: an incumbent president lost an election and accepted the result.

**Goodluck Jonathan**, facing **Muhammadu Buhari** — the former military dictator, now running for president for the fourth time as a civilian, with the persistence that distinguishes the truly motivated — lost and conceded.

He called Buhari to congratulate him before the results were officially declared, which was, by the standards of global democracy in 2015, remarkably gracious, and which Nigerians gave him considerable credit for, even those who had voted against him.

Buhari won on a platform of fighting corruption and Boko Haram. His record on both was, to use a careful word, mixed. Corruption remained extensive. Boko Haram remained active, though its territorial control was reduced. The economy fell into recession. A herdsmen-farmers conflict in the Middle Belt intensified. A second recession followed.

Buhari was re-elected in 2019 in an election that international observers described with the careful language of people who have noticed problems but are trying not to cause a diplomatic incident.

---

## PART SEVENTEEN: #ENDSARS (2020)

In October 2020, young Nigerians organized.

They organized against **SARS** — the Special Anti-Robbery Squad — a police unit with a documented record of extortion, torture, and extrajudicial killing that had become particularly notorious for targeting young men with laptops and dreadlocks on the theory that these were signs of criminality, which was a theory that the evidence did not support.

Using social media — Twitter, Instagram, WhatsApp — Nigerian youth organized protests in Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, and dozens of other cities. The protests were peaceful, remarkably well-organized, and funded by crowdsourcing. They generated international attention.

On October 20, 2020, at the **Lekki toll gate** in Lagos, soldiers opened fire on protesters.

The number of dead is disputed. The government disputed that it happened. Video footage existed. The satellite imagery existed. The witnesses existed.

The protests ended. SARS was officially disbanded. A new unit with different initials appeared and behaved in similar ways.

The young Nigerians who had protested had, however, demonstrated organizational capacity and political consciousness that would continue to develop.

---

## PART EIGHTEEN: PETER OBI AND 2023

In 2023, **Bola Tinubu**, a Yoruba political godfather from Lagos who had been a kingmaker in Nigerian politics for twenty years, won the presidential election.

He won against **Atiku Abubakar**, a northern politician who had run for president more times than is perhaps advisable, and against **Peter Obi**, a former governor of Anambra State who generated, among young urban Nigerians, the kind of enthusiasm that Nigerian elections had not previously produced.

The Peter Obi movement — the **Obidients**, as they called themselves — was notable for its youth, its educated middle class character, its social media organization, and its genuine, somewhat moving, belief that Nigeria could be different.

Tinubu won. The election was contested in court. The court confirmed Tinubu. Whether the election was free and fair remains a subject on which opinions differ sharply along lines that are not entirely unconnected to who one voted for, which is perhaps the most Nigerian thing about it.

Tinubu's first act as President was to remove the fuel subsidy, which had for decades kept petrol prices artificially low and which had been consuming vast quantities of government revenue, much of it through fraud. Removing it was economically necessary and politically catastrophic, as fuel prices increased by several hundred percent approximately overnight, and the naira collapsed, and inflation reached sixty percent.

This is the kind of thing that is right in principle and devastating in practice, which is where Nigeria so often finds itself: at the intersection of what needs to be done and what it costs to do it, borne by the people who can least afford to pay.

---

## PART NINETEEN: WHAT NIGERIA IS

Nigeria is 200 million people, approximately one in five of all Africans. It is the largest economy in Africa. It produces **Nollywood**, the world's second-largest film industry by volume, which operates on minimal budgets and maximum storytelling instinct and has made Nigerian culture a global export. It produces music — **Afrobeats**, **Afropop**, **Fela Kuti**'s Afrobeat, which is different — that plays in clubs from Lagos to London to Los Angeles.

Nigeria is a country of extraordinary writers. **Chinua Achebe** wrote *Things Fall Apart*, which is one of the best novels of the twentieth century and the most read African novel in the world. **Wole Soyinka** won the Nobel Prize in Literature. **Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie** wrote *Americanah* and *Half of a Yellow Sun* and gave the TED talk about feminism that Beyoncé sampled. **Ben Okri** won the Booker Prize. The list goes on in a way that suggests the stories that needed telling found the people to tell them.

Nigeria is a country of engineers, doctors, and mathematicians who built the NHS and American hospitals and Silicon Valley companies, and who send money home in remittances that constitute one of the largest flows of cash into Africa.

It is a country of ruinous traffic jams in Lagos, which has twenty million people and was not designed for twenty million people, or possibly for any people, but exists anyway with the determination of a city that refuses to acknowledge the possibility of stopping.

It is a country where the Niger Delta, the source of the oil wealth, remains among the most environmentally degraded places on earth, where gas flares have burned for sixty years and where people fish in water that catches fire.

It is a country where the question of what it means to be Nigerian — given that its borders were drawn by people who had not consulted it, given that its peoples spoke five hundred languages and followed Islam and Christianity and traditional religion and combinations thereof, given that its regions were so different from each other that visitors sometimes wondered if they were in the same country — that question remains genuinely open, which is either a problem or a possibility, depending on your temperament.

---

## EPILOGUE: A NOTE ON WHAT HISTORY DOES

History, if it is honest — and it is rarely entirely honest, because the people who write it were not there for most of it and were not neutral about the parts they were there for — history is not a lesson. It doesn't have a moral in the way that fables have morals.

What it has instead is this: a record of what happened to people, and what they did about it, and what the things they did led to, in an unending chain of consequences that is still going.

The Nok terracotta figures look out of their museum cases. The Benin Bronzes — many of them — look out of European and American museum cases, where they have been since 1897, when a British military expedition destroyed Benin City, burned the palace, and took approximately three thousand objects of incalculable cultural value.

Several of these objects have been returned recently, amid ongoing discussions about the rest.

The oil continues to pump. The gas continues to flare. Twenty million people continue to live in Lagos and continue to move through the traffic. Nollywood continues to make films. Afrobeats continues to take over the world, which it is doing quietly and efficiently and with excellent rhythm.

The young Nigerians who protested in October 2020 are still alive. Most of them. They have phones and opinions and organizational skills and a clear sense of what they deserve, which is better than what they have been given.

Whether they get it will determine a great deal about what the next chapter of this story contains.

The story, obviously, is not finished.

Stories like this never are.

---

*Nigeria: a country of 200 million arguments, 500 languages, 1 increasingly exasperated delta, and the unshakeable conviction, held across all ethnic groups and all political divides, that it could, should, and will, eventually, be magnificent.*

*The jury remains out.*

*The jury is taking its time.*

*The jury has opinions.*

---

*THE END (For Now)*

---

*With acknowledgment that this history, like all histories, has simplified things that were not simple, and that the people who lived these events deserve more than could fit here, and that Nigeria is large enough to contain any number of entire books, which it has, and which you should read.*

# Созидательная анархия

**Созидательная анархия** (или **«креативная анархия»**) — понятие, которое используется в нескольких контекстах:

---

## Философско-политический смысл

Восходит к идеям **анархизма** (Бакунин, Кропоткин, Прудон) — представление о том, что **разрушение старых порядков само по себе является творческим актом**, освобождающим пространство для самоорганизации.

> «Страсть к разрушению есть вместе с тем созидательная страсть» — приписывается Бакунину.

---

## В менеджменте и организационной теории

Близко к понятию **«созидательного разрушения»** Шумпетера — обновление через отказ от устаревших структур, иерархий, правил. Применяется в контексте:
- гибких организаций (agile, holacracy)
- стартап-культуры
- управления инновациями

---

## В педагогике и творчестве

Свобода от жёстких правил как условие подлинного творчества. Используется в арт-педагогике и теории креативности.

---

## Уточнение

Это понятие **не является строго устоявшимся термином** — в разных источниках оно наполняется разным смыслом.

Уточните, пожалуйста: вы встретили это понятие в каком-то конкретном тексте или контексте? Тогда я смогу ответить точнее.

This is the velocity-time graph for two cars A and B moving in the same direction. Which car has the greater acceleration? Give reason to your answer.
answer:
## Analyzing the Velocity-Time Graph

## Answer

**Car A has the greater acceleration.**

## Reason

From a velocity-time (v-t) graph, **acceleration is represented by the slope (gradient)** of the line.

$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1}$$

From the graph:
- **Car A's line** has a **steeper slope** (greater angle with the time axis)
- **Car B's line** has a **gentler/less steep slope**

Since **Slope of A > Slope of B**:

$$\boxed{a_A > a_B}$$

## Key Observations from the Graph

| Property | Car A | Car B |
|----------|-------|-------|
| Initial velocity | Lower | Higher |
| Slope of line | **Steeper** | Gentler |
| Acceleration | **Greater** | Smaller |

## Conclusion

> **Car A has greater acceleration** because the slope of its velocity-time graph is steeper than that of Car B, and slope on a v-t graph directly represents acceleration.

# GCSE Computer Science Revision Guide
## Year 11 Exam Preparation

---

## 📚 TOPIC 1: Fundamentals of Algorithms

### Key Concepts
- **Algorithm** = A set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem
- **Decomposition** = Breaking a problem into smaller parts
- **Abstraction** = Removing unnecessary details

### Searching Algorithms
| Algorithm | Best Case | Worst Case | Requirement |
|-----------|-----------|------------|-------------|
| Linear Search | O(1) | O(n) | None |
| Binary Search | O(1) | O(log n) | **Sorted list** |

### Sorting Algorithms
| Algorithm | How it works |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Bubble Sort** | Compares adjacent items, swaps if wrong order |
| **Merge Sort** | Splits list in half repeatedly, then merges |
| **Insertion Sort** | Picks each item and inserts into correct position |

### Pseudocode Example
```
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 10
    total ← total + i
ENDFOR
OUTPUT total
```

## 💻 TOPIC 2: Programming

| Type | Example |
|------|---------|
| Integer | 5, -3, 100 |
| Real/Float | 3.14, 2.5 |
| Boolean | True, False |
| String | "Hello" |
| Character | 'A' |

### Programming Constructs
- **Sequence** - Instructions in order
- **Selection** - IF/ELSE statements
- **Iteration** - FOR/WHILE loops

### Selection Example
```python
age = int(input("Enter age: "))
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")
elif age >= 13:
    print("Teenager")
else:
    print("Child")
```

### Iteration Examples
```python
# Count controlled
for i in range(5):
    print(i)

# Condition controlled
while password != "abc123":
    password = input("Enter password: ")
```

### Arrays/Lists
```python
names = ["Ali", "Beth", "Carlos"]
print(names[0])        # Ali
print(len(names))      # 3
names.append("Dana")   # Add item
```

### String Operations
```python
word = "Computer"
print(len(word))           # 8
print(word.upper())        # COMPUTER
print(word[0:4])           # Comp
print(word.substring(0,4)) # Pseudocode version
```

### Subroutines
```python
# Procedure (no return value)
def greet(name):

def add(a, b):
```

## 🔢 TOPIC 3: Data Representation

### Number Systems
| Denary | Binary | Hex |
|--------|--------|-----|
| 0 | 0000 | 0 |
| 9 | 1001 | 9 |

| 15 | 1111 | F |

### Binary Conversions
**Denary to Binary:**
```
Convert 45:
128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1
 0    0   1   0  1  1  0  1
= 00101101
```

**Binary Addition Rules:**
- 0 + 0 = 0
- 0 + 1 = 1

### Units of Storage
| Unit | Size |
|------|------|

```
File size = Width × Height × Colour depth (bits)
```

# Professional Speech: Understanding Knock-In Features of Fixed Coupon Notes (FCNs)

---

Good [morning/afternoon/evening], ladies and gentlemen.

Today, I would like to take a few moments to walk you through an important structural feature of Fixed Coupon Notes, commonly known as FCNs — specifically, the **knock-in mechanism** and how it plays a critical role in determining the redemption outcome of these instruments.

---

## The Two Types of Knock-In Features

FCNs incorporate two distinct types of knock-in features, each with its own set of conditions and implications for investors.

**The first is the European Knock-In, or EKI.**

Under this structure, a knock-in event is deemed to have occurred only if the closing price of the underlying asset — or in the case of a basket, the worst-performing underlying — falls **below its designated Knock-In Price on the Final Valuation Date**. This is a relatively more contained risk, as the observation is limited to a single, specific point in time.

**The second is the American Knock-In, or AKI.**

This structure takes a broader approach. A knock-in event is considered to have occurred if the closing price of the underlying asset, or the worst-performing underlying in a basket, falls below its Knock-In Price **on any trading day from the Trade Date through to the Final Valuation Date — both dates inclusive**. As you can appreciate, this presents a wider window of observation, and consequently, a comparatively higher probability of a knock-in event being triggered.

---

## Redemption Outcomes: What Happens at Maturity?

Now, let us turn our attention to what these knock-in events mean for you as an investor at the point of redemption.

On the **Final Valuation Date**, there are two possible outcomes:

**Outcome One: Redemption at Par**

If the price of the underlying asset closes **at or above its Strike Price** on the Final Valuation Date, **or** if a knock-in event has **never occurred** throughout the life of the note, the FCN will be **redeemed at par**. In simple terms, you will receive the full return of your principal investment. This is, of course, the favorable scenario that investors aim for.

**Outcome Two: Physical Delivery of the Underlying**

However, should a knock-in event **have occurred** at any point — whether under EKI or AKI conditions — **and** the underlying asset, or the worst-performing underlying in a basket, closes **below its Strike Price** on the Final Valuation Date, the outcome changes significantly.

In this scenario, instead of receiving your principal in cash, you will be **required to take physical delivery of the underlying asset, valued at its Strike Price**. This means you will effectively be acquiring the asset at a price that is higher than its prevailing market value, resulting in an immediate unrealized loss.

---

## Key Takeaway

Ladies and gentlemen, the knock-in feature is a defining element of FCN structures, and understanding the distinction between European and American Knock-In is essential for making informed investment decisions.

To summarize:

- **EKI** observes the underlying price only at **maturity** — a single point in time.
- **AKI** observes the underlying price **throughout the entire life** of the note — a continuous monitoring period.
- Redemption at par is achievable either when the underlying closes **above its Strike Price**, or when **no knock-in event has ever been triggered**.
- The downside scenario — physical delivery at the Strike Price — is activated only when **both conditions are met**: a knock-in event has occurred, **and** the underlying closes below its Strike Price at maturity.

As with all structured products, it is imperative that investors fully understand the risk profile and ensure that these instruments align with their overall investment objectives and risk tolerance.

Thank you for your attention. I welcome any questions you may have.

---

*Thank you.*
